specPoints.text: understand reasons for the trend in ionisation energy down Groups 1 and 2

primer.text: Groups 1 and 2 are electron donors: one or two outer electrons, willingly surrendered. This note tracks the first and second ionisation energies down both groups and explains why bigger atoms let go more easily, even though their nuclei hold more protons than their neighbours above.

lessons.title: Outer electrons and the ionisation climb
lessons.opening: Groups 1 and 2 exist to donate: one or two electrons in the outermost principal quantum shell, surrendered to form +1 or +2 ions. This lesson sets the donation in motion, names the agents, and connects the electron handover to oxidation numbers.
keyPoints: Group 1 atoms carry one electron and Group 2 atoms two, both sitting in the outermost principal quantum shell.
Donating those electrons forms ionic compounds with +1 or +2 cations.
A species that donates electrons acts as a reducing agent.
The donating metal is itself oxidised, climbing its oxidation number.
Both groups grow more reactive as the descent proceeds.

low.restatement: The outer shell holds the giveaway electrons; losing one (Group 1) or two (Group 2) leaves a stable cation, and the metal pays for the partner's reduction by being oxidised itself.
low.analogy: Two donation boxes at the door: the Group 1 box takes single coins, the Group 2 box takes pairs - and the donor's wallet (oxidation number) lightens by the same count.
low.examPointer: Link the phrases in one chain: donates electrons, therefore reducing agent, therefore oxidised itself - dropping a link costs the mark.

medium.restatement: Ionisation removes electrons from the outermost principal quantum shell; the resulting noble-gas-like cation is stabilised in ionic compounds, and the metal's reducing-agent role is exactly the electron-donation half of the redox pair.
medium.analogy: A courier handing over parcels: the courier (metal) ends each delivery lighter (oxidised) while the recipient (non-metal partner) is loaded (reduced).
medium.examPointer: For 'why are these metals reducing agents' items, answer through electron donation - never through reactivity alone.

check.stem: How many electrons sit in the outermost principal quantum shell of a Group 2 atom?

options.explanation: Group 2 atoms carry exactly two outer electrons.
Eight is a full shell, the post-donation state.

check.stem: When a Group 1 metal forms an ionic compound, what charge does its ion carry?

options.explanation: One donated electron leaves one unit of positive charge.
That is the Group 2 cation charge.
The ion is charged by definition.

check.stem: Which role does a Group 1 or 2 metal play while donating electrons?

options.text: Reducing agent, because it donates electrons

options.explanation: The metal is the central reactant.

check.stem: What happens to the metal's oxidation number as it donates its outer electrons?

options.explanation: Electron loss lifts the number by the count donated.
Donation never drives a metal negative here.

check.stem: Which direction does reactivity move down Groups 1 and 2?

options.explanation: Easier outer-electron loss powers the descent.
The shell count changes the energetics.

check.stem: State the outer-shell electron counts for Groups 1 and 2.
check.modelAnswer: Group 1 atoms hold one outer electron and Group 2 atoms hold two in their outermost principal quantum shell.

check.stem: Name the agent role of the donating metal and its own fate.
check.modelAnswer: The donating metal acts as a reducing agent and is itself oxidised.

check.stem: Explain why donating electrons makes the metal a reducing agent.
check.modelAnswer: A reducing agent reduces its partner by supplying electrons; the metal's donated electrons are exactly what the partner gains, so the metal fills the reducing role by definition.

check.stem: A Group 2 metal donates both outer electrons to two chlorine atoms. How many electrons transfer per formula unit, and what is the metal's oxidation number afterwards?
check.modelAnswer: Two electrons transfer per formula unit, leaving the metal at oxidation number +2 as its 2+ cation.

lessons.title: Reading the ionisation energy graph
lessons.opening: The graph shows both first and second ionisation energies sinking down Group 2 - and the same pattern runs through Group 1. This lesson weighs the contest between rising nuclear charge and the shielding-plus-distance pair that outvotes it.
keyPoints: The first ionisation energy removes the first outer electron; the second removes the next.
Both first and second ionisation energies decrease going down Group 2.
Group 1 shows the same downward trend in its first ionisation energy.
Nuclear charge increases down the group as protons accumulate.
Increased shielding and larger nucleus-to-electron distance outweigh the extra protons.

low.restatement: Down the group each new shell pushes the outer electrons further out and wraps them in more shielding, so removal gets cheaper despite the growing nucleus.
low.analogy: A king's herald shouting across a growing courtyard: more guards (shells) stand between the throne (nucleus) and the gate (outer electron), and every extra metre weakens the royal voice.
low.examPointer: Name BOTH outweighing factors - increased shielding AND larger distance - a single-factor answer scores half.

medium.restatement: Ionisation energy tracks the net attraction on the outermost electrons; added core shells raise shielding while radius growth lowers Coulomb attraction, together beating the proton-driven charge rise and tipping both IE1 and IE2 downward.
medium.analogy: Paying rent through an intermediary chain: each new middleman (shell) takes a cut (shields), and the longer corridor (distance) weakens the landlord's grip more than his bigger vault (more protons) compensates.
medium.examPointer: Tie the graph's two curves together: the same physics drives both ionisation energies, so quoting one curve's explanation covers both.

check.stem: What does the second ionisation energy measure?

options.text: The energy to remove the second outer electron
The energy to remove two electrons at once
options.explanation: Each ionisation is a separate step.

options.text: The energy gained when an electron arrives
The energy of the second shell
options.explanation: It measures a removal event, not a shell.

check.stem: Which trend does the Group 2 ionisation-energy graph show?

options.text: Both first and second ionisation energies decrease down the group

check.stem: Why does increasing nuclear charge fail to raise ionisation energy down the group?

options.text: Increased shielding and larger distance outweigh the extra protons
options.explanation: The two distance factors win the contest.

options.text: Distance has no effect on attraction

check.stem: Which statement about Group 1 ionisation energies is correct?

options.text: The first ionisation energy also decreases down the group
Only the second ionisation energy falls

check.stem: A student claims bigger nuclei always hold electrons tighter. What corrects the claim?

options.text: Shielding and distance can outweigh nuclear charge in heavier atoms
options.explanation: The net attraction is what matters.

options.text: Electrons get heavier down the group
Ionisation energy only depends on protons
options.explanation: Two more factors enter the balance.

check.stem: State the two factors that outweigh nuclear charge down the group.
check.modelAnswer: Increased shielding and the larger distance between outermost electrons and nucleus outweigh the growing nuclear charge.

check.stem: Quote the direction of both ionisation energies down Group 2.
check.modelAnswer: Both the first and the second ionisation energy decrease going down the group.

check.stem: Explain why easier electron removal makes the metals more reactive down the group.
check.modelAnswer: Reactivity here is electron donation, so anything that lowers the energy cost of removal - falling ionisation energies - lets atoms donate sooner and react more vigorously.

check.stem: If the first ionisation energy drops by roughly 10 percent per step down Group 2 from 900 kJ mol-1 at the top, estimate the value two steps down.
check.modelAnswer: Two 10 percent cuts leave 0.9 x 0.9 = 0.81 of 900, about 729 kJ mol-1.

glossary.definition: The energy that removes an atom's first outer electron in the gas phase.
The energy that removes the second outer electron once the first has gone.
The reduction of nuclear pull on outer electrons caused by intervening inner shells.
